title: Carry a user id through a context
description:
Implement two functions that carry a user id, a string, along with a request by storing it in a standard library context.

NewContext receives a context and a user id, and returns a new context holding that id. The context passed in is left unchanged.

FromContext receives a context and returns the stored id together with a boolean saying whether one was found. Report a missing id without panicking.

FromContext(NewContext(background, "ada")) -> "ada", true
FromContext(background) -> "", false
FromContext(NewContext(background, "")) -> "", true

The id must still be found through any context derived from the returned one, and a nearer value hides a farther one: FromContext(NewContext(NewContext(background, "ada"), "grace")) -> "grace", true.

Other packages share the same context, so your entry must be impossible for them to read, overwrite, or collide with by accident, even if they use the same string or number as a key. Define a type of your own, private to this package, for the key.
objective: Attach request-scoped data to a context behind type-safe helpers, using a private key type so packages cannot collide.

title: Run work under a time limit derived from a parent context
description:
Implement a function called RunWithin that receives a parent context, a timeout duration, a minimum duration, and a work function. The work function receives a context and returns a string. RunWithin returns that string and an error. Also define an exported error value called ErrNotEnoughTime.

Derive a new context from the parent with the given timeout. It must inherit everything from the parent, including its cancellation, its values, and an earlier deadline if the parent has one. Hand this derived context to the work function, and release its resources on every path out of RunWithin.

Before starting the work, ask the derived context when it expires. If less time remains than the minimum, do not start the work at all and return an empty string and ErrNotEnoughTime. The parent's deadline counts here, so a long timeout does not help when the parent is about to expire.

Otherwise run the work concurrently and wait for whichever comes first: the work's result, or the derived context ending. If the context ends first, return immediately with an empty string and the context's own error, even though the work may still be running.

RunWithin(background, timeout: 1s, minimum: 0, work returns "done") -> "done", no error
RunWithin(background, timeout: 20ms, minimum: 0, work never returns) -> "", the deadline-exceeded error
RunWithin(parent cancelled after 20ms, timeout: 1m, minimum: 0, work never returns) -> "", the cancelled error
RunWithin(background, timeout: 50ms, minimum: 1h, any work) -> "", ErrNotEnoughTime, and the work never starts
RunWithin(parent expiring in 100ms, timeout: 1h, minimum: 1m, any work) -> "", ErrNotEnoughTime, and the work never starts
objective: Practice deriving a context with a timeout, releasing it, checking its deadline before starting, and waiting on its done signal.

title: Take the first result and cancel the other workers
description:
Implement a function called FirstResult that receives a parent context and a list of worker functions. Each worker receives a context and returns a string and an error. FirstResult returns a string and an error.

Start every worker at the same time, all sharing one context that can be cancelled and that is derived from the parent. As soon as one worker succeeds, return its string with no error and signal the remaining workers to stop through that shared context. A worker that fails does not end the race, so keep waiting for the others.

FirstResult(background, [worker waits until told to stop, worker returns "fast"]) -> "fast", no error, and the first worker is told to stop
FirstResult(background, [worker fails with "broken", worker returns "survivor" after 20ms]) -> "survivor", no error

If every worker fails, return an empty string and the error of the worker that failed last:
FirstResult(background, [worker fails with "late" after 30ms, worker fails with "early"]) -> "", "late"

An empty list of workers returns an empty string and an error. If the parent is cancelled, return at once with an empty string and the cancelled error, even when a worker ignores its context and has not finished.

A worker that finishes after FirstResult has already returned must still be able to report its result and exit. It must never stay stuck forever, and the hidden tests check that no goroutine is left behind.
objective: Practice broadcasting one cancellation to many goroutines, and collecting their results so that none of them leaks.

title: Make an http request that stops when its context does
description:
Implement a function called HTTPDo that receives a context, an http request, and a callback. The callback receives the http response and the error from performing the request, and returns an error. HTTPDo returns an error.

Tie the request to the context so that cancelling the context aborts the request itself. Perform the request with the default http client on a separate goroutine, and pass both of its results straight to the callback. Closing the response body is the callback's job.

Then wait for whichever comes first: the callback returning, or the context ending.

If the callback returns first, return its error:
HTTPDo(background, request, callback returns "boom") -> "boom"
HTTPDo(background, request, callback reads the body and returns no error) -> no error

If the context ends first, the callback may still be running and may still be using data that belongs to the caller. So wait until it has returned, and only then return the context's own error, discarding the callback's:
HTTPDo(context cancelled while the callback is running, request, callback returns "from the callback") -> the cancelled error, and only after the callback has finished
HTTPDo(context with a 20ms timeout, request to a server that never replies, callback returns the error it received) -> the deadline-exceeded error
objective: Practice tying an http request to a context and waiting for in-flight work before reporting cancellation, so a caller can safely use what the callback wrote.
